title: Tie Your Camel
text:
In early Islam, trust in God, called tawakkul, was among the virtues most praised. A believer was to rely on God for his sustenance and safety, not on his own cleverness. But how far should that trust go?

The collection of hadith compiled by al-Tirmidhi preserves a short exchange on this question, reported by Anas ibn Malik, a companion of the Prophet. A man came to the Prophet with his camel. For a desert people, a camel was a means of travel, a store of wealth and sometimes the difference between life and death, and an animal left loose could easily wander off or be stolen.

The man asked what he should do. Should he tie up his camel and trust in God? Or should he leave it untied and trust in God?

The Prophet answered: tie her, and trust.

The answer was short, and it has traveled far. It is quoted across the Muslim world and beyond, often in the form "Trust in God, but tie your camel," as a reminder that faith and good sense are not opposites. Doing everything sensible within your power is part of trusting, not a sign of doubt.
lesson: Hope and faith are no substitute for basic precautions. Do your part fully, lock the door and check the plan, and then let go of what is outside your control.
people: The Prophet Muhammad, a man with a camel
source: Al-Tirmidhi, Jami (Sunan) al-Tirmidhi, Book of the Description of the Day of Judgment, hadith 2517, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
caveat: Al-Tirmidhi himself called this hadith unusual (gharib); later scholars differ on how strong its chain of transmission is.
